tagline: A prophet of the rebuilding: night visions, a call to return, and oracles of a coming king whose humility and piercing the Gospels saw fulfilled in Jesus.
overview:
Zechariah is the longest of the twelve shorter prophetic books that close the Old Testament, and many readers find it the most difficult. It opens in Jerusalem around 520 BC, less than twenty years after the first exiles came home from Babylon. The temple still lay in ruins, the returned community was small and poor, and the great promises of the earlier prophets seemed a long way off. Zechariah, working alongside the prophet Haggai, called the people to return to God and to finish rebuilding his house, and he told them what he had seen in a single night: eight visions of horses, horns, lampstands, a flying scroll, and chariots, each explained by an angel, all saying that God had not forgotten Jerusalem.

The book falls into two halves. Chapters 1 to 8 are dated to the reign of the Persian king Darius I and are full of the rebuilding: the visions, the cleansing and crowning of the high priest Joshua, words to the governor Zerubbabel, and a set of promises that turns the people's mourning fasts into feasts. Chapters 9 to 14 carry no dates and read differently. They are two collections of oracles, each headed with the word for a prophetic burden, about a king coming to Zion, shepherds good and worthless, a Jerusalem besieged and rescued, a fountain opened for cleansing, and a final day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.

The book matters to Christians out of all proportion to its size, because the Gospel writers turned to it again and again to tell the story of Jesus's last week. The king riding a donkey (9:9), the thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter (11:12-13), the one who is pierced (12:10), and the shepherd struck so the sheep scatter (13:7) all appear in the passion narratives. Zechariah is where the New Testament learned to speak of a humble, rejected, and pierced king.
author:
The book names its prophet as Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo (1:1). The books of Ezra call him simply the son of Iddo (Ezra 5:1; 6:14), perhaps because his grandfather was the better-known figure or because his father died young, and Nehemiah 12:16 lists a Zechariah as head of the priestly family of Iddo in the next generation. If these are the same man, Zechariah was a priest as well as a prophet, which fits his deep interest in the temple, the high priest, and purity.

That Zechariah stands behind chapters 1 to 8 is widely agreed. Chapters 9 to 14 are debated. They contain no dates, no night visions, no interpreting angel, and no mention of Zechariah, Joshua, Zerubbabel, or the temple rebuilding; they are written largely in poetry and speak of Greece (9:13), Assyria, and Egypt. Most critical scholars since the nineteenth century attribute them to one or more later, unnamed prophets (often called Second Zechariah, sometimes divided again into chapters 9 to 11 and 12 to 14), noting that the heading used at 9:1 and 12:1 also opens Malachi, so that the Twelve may end with three anonymous oracle collections. Some older scholars, prompted partly by Matthew's attribution of the thirty pieces of silver to Jeremiah, placed chapters 9 to 11 before the exile. Many conservative scholars hold that Zechariah wrote the whole book, and that the change of style reflects a different genre and a later stage of his ministry. Scholars on every side have also traced real connections between the halves: the cleansing of the land, Jerusalem's future, the shepherd-leaders, and the nations coming to worship. The book as it stands was received as one prophetic book, and it is read here that way.
date:
Chapters 1 to 8 are dated precisely by the reign of Darius I of Persia. Zechariah's first word came in the eighth month of Darius's second year, October or November of 520 BC (1:1). The night visions came on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of that year, around February 519 BC (1:7). The question about fasting came in Darius's fourth year, in the ninth month, around December 518 BC (7:1). The temple was finished in Darius's sixth year, in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).

The date of chapters 9 to 14 depends on the authorship question. Those who hold that Zechariah wrote them place them later in his own life, perhaps in the early fifth century BC, when Persia was at war with the Greek cities. Many critical scholars place them in the fifth or fourth century BC, and some later still, reading the mention of Greece and the march of chapter 9 against the conquests of Alexander the Great in 333 and 332 BC. A smaller number have argued for a date before the exile for parts of chapters 9 to 11.
setting:
In 539 BC the Persian king Cyrus took Babylon, and within a year he allowed exiled Judeans to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 1). The returned community set up the altar and laid the temple's foundations, but opposition from neighbors and their own discouragement stopped the work for about sixteen years (Ezra 3 and 4). When Darius I seized the Persian throne in 522 BC, revolts broke out across the empire before he secured his rule. In 520 BC, in the second year of his reign, Haggai and then Zechariah urged the people to start building again (Ezra 5:1-2). Judah was then a small province of the Persian Empire, governed by Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, with Joshua son of Jehozadak as high priest.

The first readers were a disappointed people. The land was poor and the harvests thin. Jerusalem had few inhabitants and broken walls. The throne of David was empty, and the prophets had promised far more than this. The new temple looked like nothing beside the memory of Solomon's (Haggai 2:3). Zechariah speaks into that gap between promise and experience.
purpose: Zechariah wrote to call a discouraged community back to God and to the work in front of them. The book opens with a summons, return to me and I will return to you (1:3), and a warning not to repeat the fathers' refusal to listen. The visions assure the people that God rules the nations, that he is jealous for Jerusalem, that he will cleanse his people's guilt, and that the temple will be finished by his Spirit rather than by force. Chapters 7 and 8 insist that fasting means nothing without justice and mercy toward the widow, the orphan, the stranger, and the poor. Chapters 9 to 14 lift the reader's eyes further, to a future in which God will send a king, judge the false shepherds, cleanse his people through grief and a fountain of cleansing, and gather the nations to worship him in a holy Jerusalem. The book was written for people who had come home and still waited for the fullness of what home was supposed to be.
story: Zechariah stands near the end of the Old Testament story. Before him lie the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, the exile in Babylon, and the return under Cyrus told in Ezra 1 to 3. His ministry overlaps Haggai's and belongs to the same moment as Ezra 5 and 6, when the second temple was built. After him come the work of Ezra and Nehemiah in the fifth century BC and the last of the prophets, Malachi. Then the Old Testament falls silent for about four centuries, and the next time these streets appear in Scripture, a king rides into Jerusalem on a donkey while the crowd sings.
christ: Few Old Testament books are drawn on more heavily in the Gospels' account of Jesus's last days. Matthew and John both say that Jesus's entry into Jerusalem on a donkey fulfilled Zechariah 9:9 (Matthew 21:4-5; John 12:14-15). Jesus himself cited Zechariah 13:7 on the night of his arrest, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27). Matthew connects the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas, returned to the temple and used to buy a potter's field, with Zechariah 11:12-13, though he credits the words to Jeremiah (Matthew 27:3-10). John sees Zechariah 12:10 fulfilled when a soldier pierced Jesus's side (John 19:37), and Revelation 1:7 applies the same verse to his return. The Branch who will build the temple and be a priest on his throne (3:8; 6:12-13), the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness (13:1), and the living waters flowing from Jerusalem (14:8) have all been read as pointing to Christ, while Revelation draws on Zechariah's horses, lampstands, and olive trees (Revelation 6; 11:4). Taken together, the book gives the New Testament its picture of a king who comes in humility, is valued at a slave's price, is pierced by his own people, and yet reigns over all the earth.
reading:
Read chapters 1 to 6 as apocalyptic vision: symbolic scenes interpreted by an angel, closer to a dream than to a report. Don't press every detail for a hidden meaning; ask what the angel says the vision means, and let that carry the weight. The visions move in a pattern, beginning and ending with horses patrolling the earth, with the visions of the high priest and the lampstand at the center. Read chapters 7 and 8 as prophetic sermons, and chapters 9 to 14 as poetic oracles about the future, full of older prophetic language from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

Two cautions help. First, the later chapters are highly figurative. Readers disagree whether their battles and blessings refer to events after the exile, to the coming of Christ and the church, to a future restoration of Israel, or to several of these, and it's wise to hold detailed timetables loosely. Second, the text of Zechariah is difficult in places, and translations differ; where a note says the Hebrew is uncertain, it is. The steady line through all of it is simple: the LORD has returned to his people, he will cleanse them, and he will be king over all the earth.

structure.title: A call to return
structure.summary: Zechariah's first message, in late 520 BC, calls the people to return to the LORD and not to repeat their fathers' refusal to listen to the prophets.

structure.title: Eight night visions and a crowning
structure.summary: In one night Zechariah sees eight visions, from the horsemen among the myrtles to the four chariots, each interpreted by an angel. They promise God's return to Jerusalem, judgment on the nations, the cleansing of the high priest and the land, and the completion of the temple, and they close with a symbolic crown and a word about the Branch.

structure.title: Fasts turned to feasts
structure.summary: A question about fasting, in 518 BC, prompts a call to justice and mercy, a reminder of why the exile came, and ten promises of a restored Jerusalem to which the nations will come seeking God.

structure.title: The first burden: the coming king and the rejected shepherd
structure.summary: God marches against Israel's neighbors, a humble king rides into Zion, the scattered people are gathered, and a prophetic shepherd is rejected and valued at thirty pieces of silver.

structure.title: The second burden: Jerusalem cleansed and the LORD as king
structure.summary: Jerusalem is besieged and rescued, the people mourn for the one they have pierced, a fountain is opened to cleanse them, the shepherd is struck, and the LORD becomes king over all the earth.

themes.title: Return
themes.body: The book opens with God's invitation, return to me and I will return to you (1:3), and the whole of it unfolds that promise. The people are to turn from the ways of their fathers; God, in turn, comes back to Jerusalem with mercy, to live among them. Zechariah insists that the exile was real judgment for real refusal (7:11-14), and that God's return is pure mercy rather than a reward earned.

themes.title: Cleansing
themes.body: Zechariah's concern is not only a rebuilt building but a purified people. The high priest's filthy garments are removed (chapter 3), wickedness is carried away to Babylon in a basket (chapter 5), a fountain is opened for sin and impurity (13:1), and at the end even the cooking pots of Jerusalem are holy (14:20-21). God does not simply return to the people as they are; he makes them fit for his presence.

themes.title: Temple and leadership
themes.body: The first half turns on the rebuilding of the temple and on the two leaders of the community, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor from David's line. The Branch will build the temple and bear royal splendor (6:12-13), and the work will succeed by God's Spirit rather than by military power (4:6). The second half turns to shepherds: faithless leaders who fleece the flock, and a shepherd whom the people reject.

themes.title: The king who comes humbly
themes.body: Zechariah's king comes riding a donkey, righteous and humble (9:9), and he speaks peace to the nations. The same half of the book speaks of a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver and of one who is pierced and mourned. The book holds together royal victory and suffering rejection in a way that puzzled its readers until the Gospels read both in the life of one man.

themes.title: The nations and the kingdom of God
themes.body: The nations who scattered Judah will be judged (1:18-21), but many nations will also join themselves to the LORD (2:11), ten men will grasp the robe of a Jew to go with him to God (8:23), and survivors of the nations will come up each year to worship the King (14:16). The book ends with the LORD as king over all the earth and holiness spread into every corner of ordinary life.

keyChapters.why: The call to return and the first night vision, in which God declares that he is jealous for Jerusalem and will return to it with mercy.
Joshua the high priest, accused by Satan, is stripped of filthy garments and clothed in clean ones, a picture of forgiveness, and the promised Branch is announced.
The golden lampstand and the two olive trees, with the book's best-known word: not by might nor by power, but by God's Spirit.
Ten promises of a restored Jerusalem, where old people sit in the streets, children play, fasts become feasts, and the nations come seeking God.
The king who comes to Zion humble and riding on a donkey, the text the Gospels quote at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem.
The shepherd who is rejected and paid thirty pieces of silver, which Matthew connects with Judas's betrayal.
The spirit of grace poured out and the people's mourning for the one they have pierced, cited by John at the cross.
The day of the LORD, living waters flowing from Jerusalem, and the LORD as king over all the earth.

parts.body:
Zechariah is the eleventh of the twelve shorter prophets and the longest, fourteen chapters, and many readers find it the hardest. It opens in Jerusalem around 520 BC, less than twenty years after the first exiles came home from Babylon. The temple still lay in ruins, the community was small and poor, and the great promises of the earlier prophets seemed far away. Zechariah, working beside Haggai, called the people to return to God and to finish rebuilding his house. ‘Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you’ (1:3).

He told them what he had seen in a single night: eight visions of horses, horns, a measuring line, a lampstand, a flying scroll and chariots, each explained by an angel, all saying that God had not forgotten Jerusalem. ‘Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts’ (4:6).

The second half, chapters 9 to 14, carries no dates and reads differently: a king coming to Zion humble and riding on a donkey (9:9), shepherds good and worthless, a Jerusalem besieged and rescued, one who is pierced, a fountain opened for cleansing, and a last day when ‘the LORD will become King over all the earth’ (14:9). Few Old Testament books are drawn on more in the Gospels' account of Jesus' last days.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and soon allowed the exiles to return and rebuild the temple. They set up the altar and laid the foundations, but opposition and discouragement stopped the work for about sixteen years. When Darius I seized the Persian throne in 522 BC, revolts broke out across the empire before he secured it. In 520 BC, his second year, Haggai and then Zechariah urged the people to build again. Judah was a small Persian province, governed by Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, with Joshua son of Jehozadak as high priest.

The first readers were a disappointed people. The land was poor, Jerusalem thinly settled and its walls broken, and the throne of David empty. The temple was finished in Darius's sixth year, 515 BC.

The book names its prophet as ‘Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo’ (1:1). Ezra calls him the son of Iddo, perhaps because his grandfather was better known, and Nehemiah lists a Zechariah as head of the priestly family of Iddo in the next generation. If these are the same man, Zechariah was a priest as well as a prophet, which fits his interest in the temple, the high priest and purity.

That Zechariah stands behind chapters 1 to 8 is widely agreed. Chapters 9 to 14 are debated, and this site takes no side. They contain no dates, no night visions, no interpreting angel and no mention of Zechariah, Joshua, Zerubbabel or the rebuilding, and they speak of Greece (9:13). Most critical scholars since the nineteenth century give them to one or more later prophets, often called Second Zechariah, noting that the heading at 9:1 and 12:1 also opens Malachi. Some older scholars placed chapters 9 to 11 before the exile. Many conservative scholars hold that Zechariah wrote the whole book, later in his life.

Chapters 1 to 8 are dated by Darius's reign: the first word in late 520 BC (1:1), the night visions about February 519 BC (1:7), the question about fasting about December 518 BC (7:1). Those who hold that Zechariah wrote chapters 9 to 14 place them in the early fifth century BC; many critical scholars place them in the fifth or fourth century, some reading chapter 9 against the conquests of Alexander the Great in 333 and 332 BC.

Chapters 1 to 6 are eight night visions, symbolic scenes explained by an angel, closer to a dream than a report. They begin and end with horses patrolling the earth, and the visions of the high priest and the lampstand stand at the center. Do not press every detail for a hidden meaning; ask what the angel says the vision means, and let that carry the weight.

Chapters 7 and 8 are sermons about fasting, justice and the city's future. Chapters 9 to 14 are two collections of poetic oracles, each headed burden, full of language from Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

The later chapters are highly figurative, and readers disagree whether their battles and promises refer to events after the exile, to Christ and the church, to a future restoration of Israel, or to several of these. Hold detailed timetables loosely. The text is hard in places and translations differ. The steady line through it all is simple: the LORD has returned to his people, he will cleanse them, and he will be king over all the earth.

The first vision shows horsemen among myrtle trees who report that the earth is at rest, while Jerusalem still lies in ruins. The angel asks how long, and God answers that he is jealous for Jerusalem and will return to it with mercy. Four horns that scattered Judah are met by four craftsmen who throw them down (chapter 1). A young man goes to measure Jerusalem, but the city will be too full for walls: ‘For I will be a wall of fire around it, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory within it’ (2:5).

At the center, Joshua the high priest stands in filthy clothes with the accuser beside him. The LORD rebukes the accuser, Joshua is given clean robes, and God promises to bring his servant the Branch and remove the land's guilt in a single day (chapter 3). A golden lampstand fed by two olive trees is a word to Zerubbabel: the temple will be finished by God's Spirit, and no one should despise ‘the day of small things’ (4:10).

A flying scroll carries a curse on thieves and perjurers. A woman called Wickedness is shut in a measuring basket and carried away to Shinar; the Hebrew word for wickedness is feminine, and the two figures who carry it away are also women, so the vision does not set women against God (chapter 5). Last, four chariots go out over the earth, and a crown is set on Joshua's head as a sign of a man called the Branch, who will build the temple and be a priest on his throne (chapter 6).

Two years later, people from Bethel ask whether they should keep fasting in the fifth month, as they had for years in mourning for the temple. God answers with a question: were those fasts really for him? Then he repeats what the earlier prophets said: ‘Administer true justice. Show loving devotion and compassion to one another’ (7:9), and do not oppress the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor. That refusal, hearts made hard as flint, is why the exile came.

God does not forbid the fasts. In chapter 8 he promises to turn them into feasts. Jerusalem will be the City of Truth, and ‘Old men and old women will again sit along the streets of Jerusalem’ (8:4), and the streets will be full of children playing. The chapter ends with the nations: ten people from every language will take hold of a Jew's robe and ask to go with him, because they have heard that God is with his people (8:23).

parts.h: Your King comes, humble and riding on a donkey
parts.body:
The second half opens with the LORD's judgment moving down through Syria, Phoenicia and Philistia while he guards his own house. Then the call: “Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion! Shout in triumph, O Daughter of Jerusalem! See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (9:9). He will cut off the chariot and the war horse, and proclaim peace to the nations.

The chapter also celebrates God's victory over the nations, and readers feel the tension. The warfare is God's own action against the powers that oppressed his people, not a license for human aggression, and even the Philistines become a remnant for God (9:7).

Chapters 10 and 11 turn to shepherds. The people have trusted idols and diviners and are like sheep without a shepherd. The prophet is told to shepherd a flock marked for slaughter. He takes two staffs, Favor and Union, and when he asks for his wages they weigh out ‘thirty pieces of silver’ (11:12), and the LORD tells him to throw it to the potter, ‘this magnificent price at which they valued me’ (11:13). The prophet breaks both staffs.

parts.h: The one they pierced, and a fountain opened
parts.body:
The second collection opens with Jerusalem made a heavy stone to the nations gathered against it. Then God says, ‘I will pour out on the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayer, and they will look on Me, the One they have pierced’ (12:10). They will mourn as for an only child, every family apart.

The standard Hebrew text has the people look on the speaker, God himself, and some manuscripts read to him. Many modern scholars accept the first person as the harder and better reading. How God can be pierced is read in several ways: figuratively, as grieving God by rejecting him; or of God's representative, perhaps the rejected shepherd of chapter 11. These notes leave the readings as readings.

‘On that day a fountain will be opened to the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and impurity’ (13:1). Idols and false prophecy will be removed. Then the LORD calls a sword against his own shepherd: ‘Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered’ (13:7). A third will be brought through fire and refined like silver, and God will say they are his people, and they will say the LORD is their God (13:9).

parts.h: The LORD will be King over all the earth
parts.body:
In chapter 14 the nations gather against Jerusalem and the city falls. These notes name the cruelties of that war as crimes and do not describe them. Then the LORD himself goes out to fight, standing on the Mount of Olives as it splits in two. Living water flows from Jerusalem east and west, summer and winter. ‘On that day the LORD will become King over all the earth’ (14:9). The survivors of the nations go up every year to worship him at the Feast of Tabernacles. Everything becomes holy, from the bells on the horses to the cooking pots.

Christians read the chapter in different ways, and this site takes no side. Many dispensational and other premillennial interpreters take it as a prediction of real future events: a final siege of Jerusalem, Christ's return to the Mount of Olives, and his reign on earth. Many amillennial and other interpreters read it as prophetic imagery drawn from Israel's world, the temple, the feasts and the enemy nations, describing the triumph of God's kingdom fulfilled in Christ, the gathering of the nations into the church, and the new creation. Others see both a present fulfillment and a future completion.

The chapter gives no warrant for violence against any people, and it makes no claim about any modern state, city or border.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Zechariah
parts.body:
The Gospels draw on Zechariah at four places, and these notes draw only those. Matthew and John say that Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on a donkey fulfilled 9:9: ‘See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey’ (Matthew 21:5; compare John 12:15). Jesus himself cited 13:7 on the night of his arrest: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered’ (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27).

Matthew connects the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas, returned to the temple and used to buy a potter's field, with 11:12-13, though he credits the words to Jeremiah (Matthew 27:9-10). Many scholars explain that the quotation blends Zechariah's wording with themes from Jeremiah, a potter and a field bought, and names the more prominent prophet, as Mark 1:2-3 names Isaiah for words that blend Malachi and Isaiah; others suggest Jeremiah stood first in some arrangements of the prophets. John says that when a soldier pierced Jesus' side, ‘They will look on the One they have pierced’ (John 19:37), and Revelation applies the same verse to his return (Revelation 1:7).

These are the New Testament's own lines from Zechariah. The book's mourning for the pierced one is spoken of Israel's own house of David and Jerusalem, and the New Testament never uses it to blame the Jewish people.

Read the visions as visions, and let the angel's explanations carry the weight. Read chapters 7 and 8 as sermons about justice and joy. Read chapters 9 to 14 as poetry about the future, and hold timetables loosely.

Notice the steady line: God returns to his people, cleanses them, and becomes king over all the earth. Notice too the king the book promises, humble and riding on a donkey, and the shepherd who is struck.

And notice that the book ends with ordinary things made holy, the bells on the horses and the pots in the kitchen. The holiness of the temple spills into the whole of life.

hard.line: God was a little angry, but the nations added to the calamity.
Who is the one the LORD of Hosts has sent, who speaks as God?
Joshua in filthy clothes, and the accuser rebuked.
The two olive trees, the two anointed ones.
Wickedness pictured as a woman: a feminine noun, carried away by women.
A crown on Joshua the priest rather than on Zerubbabel.
Is God rejecting fasting and religious practice?
The humble king on a donkey, and the Gospels' entry into Jerusalem.
A king of peace, and a chapter that celebrates God's victory over the nations.
Thirty pieces of silver, and why Matthew names Jeremiah.
They will look on God, or on another, whom they have pierced.
Parents who turn on a child who prophesies falsely: hyperbole, and no rule for any family.
Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter.
A final battle on the Mount of Olives: literal future, imagery, or both?

words.line: Eight symbolic scenes seen in one night, each explained by an angel (1:7 to 6:15).
The heavenly messenger who speaks for God and is also distinguished from him (1:11-12; 3:1-6).
Ha-satan, who stands to accuse Joshua and is rebuked by the LORD (3:1-2).
God's servant, a sprout from David's line, who will build the temple (3:8; 6:12).
The vision of God's Spirit supplying the work, and the two anointed ones (4:2-14).

words.word: Not by might nor by power
words.line: The word to Zerubbabel: the temple will be finished by God's Spirit (4:6).
The humble beginnings no one should despise (4:10).
Jerusalem's new name when God returns to dwell in it (8:3).
Massa, the heading of the two collections in chapters 9 to 14 (9:1; 12:1).
Zion's king who comes righteous and victorious, riding on a donkey (9:9).
The two staffs the prophet breaks, ending covenant and brotherhood (11:7-14).
The wages weighed out for the shepherd and thrown to the potter (11:12-13).
The one Jerusalem looks on and mourns as for an only child (12:10).
Cleansing from sin and impurity for David's house and Jerusalem (13:1).
The words once on the high priest's turban, written on the horses' bells (14:20).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The city God returns to, the City of Truth (8:3); the Mount of Olives stands to its east (14:4).

places.line: Its people sent to ask whether they should keep fasting (7:2).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: Where the word against the nations comes to rest (9:1).

places.name: Tyre
places.line: The port that heaped up silver like dust and will be burned (9:3-4).

places.name: Sidon
places.line: Tyre's sister city, named with it (9:2).

places.name: Ashdod
places.line: A Philistine city where a mixed people will live (9:6).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan to which God will bring his scattered people (10:10). Drawn roughly, as a region.

places.name: The Jordan
places.line: Its thickets, home of lions, are ruined (11:3).

teaching.mapNote: Eight places are drawn, each at a point already used on this site's maps; Gilead roughly, as a region. The Mount of Olives, Hadrach, Hamath, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron, Lebanon, Bashan, Shinar, Babylon, Egypt and Assyria are not placed in this site's records and are left off. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
